section.title: Stewards of God's Grace
section.sectionRationale: Peter draws out the practical fruit of Christ's suffering: a decisive break with the old life of sin and a new life for God's will, lived in view of the coming judgment and the nearness of the end. That horizon presses believers not to panic but to pray, love, and serve one another as faithful stewards of God's varied grace.
section.thesis: Because Christ suffered in the body, believers arm themselves to be done with sin and live for God's will, and because the end of all things is near, they are clear-minded in prayer, fervent in love, and faithful in using their gifts as stewards of God's manifold grace, so that in everything God is glorified through Jesus Christ.
section.frameNote: Two movements: done with sin and living for God's will before the Judge, verses 1 to 6; and the nearness of the end, love and stewardship of grace, verses 7 to 11.

units.label: Done with sin, living for God's will
units.note: before the Judge of living and dead

verses.text: Therefore, since Christ suffered in His body, {{hoplizo|arm yourselves}} with the same resolve, because anyone who has suffered in his body is done with sin.
Consequently, he does not live out his remaining time on earth for human passions, but for the will of God.
For you have spent enough time in the past carrying out the same desires as the Gentiles: living in debauchery, lust, drunkenness, orgies, carousing, and detestable idolatry.
Because of this, they consider it strange of you not to plunge with them into the same flood of reckless indiscretion, and they heap abuse on you.
But they will have to give an account to Him who is ready to judge the living and the dead.
That is why the gospel was preached even to those who are now dead, so that they might be judged as men in the flesh, but live according to God in the spirit.

units.label: Love and serve as stewards of grace
units.note: the end of all things is near

verses.text: The {{telos|end of all things}} is near. Therefore be clear-minded and sober, so that you can pray.
Above all, {{agape|love one another deeply}}, because love covers over a multitude of sins.
Show hospitality to one another without complaining.
As good {{oikonomoi|stewards}} of the {{poikile|manifold grace}} of God, each of you should use whatever {{charisma|gift}} he has received to serve one another.

If anyone speaks, he should speak as one conveying the words of God. If anyone serves, he should serve with the strength God provides, so that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom be the glory and the power forever and ever. Amen.

hoplizo.gloss: To arm oneself, to take up weapons for battle. Believers are to arm themselves with the same mind or resolve that Christ had in His suffering. The Christian life is pictured as warfare, and the weapon is a settled willingness to suffer rather than sin, a resolve that has broken decisively with the old life.

telos.gloss: The end, the goal or consummation. Peter says the end of all things has drawn near. This is not a cause for panic but for clear-headed prayer and love. The nearness of the end gives the present its weight and urgency, focusing the church on what truly matters as history moves toward its appointed goal.

agape.gloss: Self-giving love that seeks the good of others. Peter says, above all, love one another earnestly, for love covers a multitude of sins. In a community under pressure, fervent love is the first priority, bearing with one another's faults and knitting the church together as the end draws near.

oikonomoi.gloss: A steward, a household manager entrusted with another's resources. Believers are stewards of God's grace, responsible to use what He has given for the good of others. A steward owns nothing and must give account; so gifts are held in trust from God and deployed for the household of faith, not for self.

poikile.gloss: Manifold, many-colored, varied grace. God's grace comes in diverse forms, distributed in different gifts to different believers. The word pictures grace like a richly varied tapestry; no one holds it all, so the church needs every member's gift to display the full spectrum of God's giving.

charisma.gloss: A gift of grace, a Spirit-given ability for service. Each believer has received some charisma to use in serving others. The gifts are not for personal display but for the common good, so that whether one speaks or serves, God is glorified through Jesus Christ, the giver and goal of every gift.

basic.context: Because Christ suffered, Peter says, arm yourselves with the same resolve: be done with sin and live the rest of your life for God's will, not for the old cravings. Your former friends think it strange that you no longer join their wild living, and they insult you, but they will answer to God, the Judge of the living and the dead. Then Peter lifts the horizon: the end of all things is near. So keep clear heads and pray. Above all, love one another deeply, be hospitable, and use whatever gift God has given you to serve others, as faithful stewards of His varied grace, so that in everything God gets the glory through Jesus Christ.
basic.hermeneutics: Peter uses the coming judgment and the nearness of the end not to stir fear or speculation but to fuel holy, loving, useful living now. Two lines need care. Anyone who has suffered in the body is done with sin, verse 1, means the settled resolve to suffer rather than sin marks a decisive break with the old life. And the gospel preached to those now dead, verse 6, most likely means believers who heard the gospel while alive and have since died, so that though judged in the body by death, they live before God.
basic.originalLanguages: Since Christ suffered, believers hoplizo, arm themselves, with the same resolve, done with sin. The telos, the end of all things, is near, so they pray and above all show agape, love, which covers many sins. As oikonomoi, stewards, of the poikile charis, the manifold grace of God, each uses his charisma, his gift, to serve others.
basic.typology: The steward of the household reflects the whole biblical picture of God's people as managers of what He owns, from Adam tending the garden to servants entrusted with talents. And the coming Judge of the living and the dead fulfils the Old Testament expectation of the day of the Lord, now centered on Christ.
basic.christ: Christ's suffering is the pattern and power for the believer's break with sin. He is the one through whom God is glorified in all our serving, and to whom belong glory and power forever. As the Judge of the living and the dead, He is the one before whom both mockers and martyrs will finally stand.
basic.god: God is the Judge of the living and the dead, before whom all give account. He is the giver of manifold grace and varied gifts, and the one who supplies the strength for service. He is the God whose will now directs the believer's life and whose glory is the goal of everything. He is generous, sovereign, and worthy of all glory and power forever.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 6 speaks of dying to sin and living to God. Romans 12 and 1 Corinthians 12 describe varied gifts for serving the body. Proverbs 10 says love covers all offenses. And James 5 says the coming of the Lord is near, urging patient, prayerful living.
basic.oneStory: The whole Bible moves toward the end, when the Judge of all sets things right. Christ has suffered and risen, sin's grip is broken, and the church now lives in the last stretch of the story. In this in-between time God's people love, pray, and serve as stewards of His grace, so that when the end comes, He is glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom belong glory and power forever.

context.literary:
The passage has two panels with a turning word between them. Verses 1 to 6 look back and ask what the believer has left behind, and verses 7 to 11 look ahead and ask what the believer does with the time that remains. The bridge is 'the end of all things is near', which gathers the judgment of verse 5 and sends it forward into the practical life of the community.

The first panel is built around a contrast of two lives. On one side stands 'human passions', verse 2, filled out by a catalog of six items in verse 3. On the other side is 'the will of God'. Peter lets the old life be named plainly, then shows it from the inside: it is a flood, verse 4, a rushing stream that sweeps people along and that those who stand apart will be insulted for resisting. Verses 5 and 6 close the panel with the courtroom, the Judge of the living and the dead, so that mockery gives way to accountability.

The second panel is made of a string of short commands, each tied to the one before. Be clear-minded so that you can pray. Above all love, and love will lead to hospitality without complaint. Hospitality is one of the forms gifts take, and gifts are described in verse 10 as stewardship. Verse 11 then divides all gifts into two classes, speaking and serving, so that no one can say they have nothing to give.

The passage ends with a doxology, 'to whom be the glory and the power forever and ever. Amen'. It is the first of two such endings in the letter, the other being 5:11. The purpose clause 'so that in all things God may be glorified' controls everything before it: the pursuit of holiness, prayer, love, hospitality, speech and service all aim at one end.

In the letter as a whole, this section sits between the great doctrinal statement of 3:18-22 and the call to endure fiery trials in 4:12 and following. It draws the lesson from Christ's suffering and prepares for the sharper word about persecution.
context.historical:
Peter's readers lived in cities where social life was soaked in the worship of local gods and the emperor. Trade guilds, civic banquets, family festivals and temple feasts all involved religious acts and often the drinking and licence that belonged to them. The six words of verse 3 cover that world, and they included the heavy drinking parties and the processions with revelry that were part of public religious life. A believer who stayed away from them was making a statement, and the neighbors noticed.

The phrase 'they consider it strange' reflects a real social cost. In a world where belonging depended on joining in, refusing to join was seen as arrogance or disloyalty. Pagan writers of the period commonly accused the Christians of hating humanity because they would not share in these customs. Peter's language, 'they heap abuse', is the speech of people offended by a silent rebuke.

'The end of all things is near' was spoken in a church that lived in expectation of Christ's return. Paul and James used the same nearness, Romans 13:11-12 and James 5:8. It was not a calculation of dates but a way of seeing every day in the light of the Lord's coming. Peter uses it to produce sobriety, not frenzy.

Hospitality had particular weight. There were few reliable inns, and those that existed were often unsafe and associated with immoral behavior. Traveling believers, including messengers, teachers and refugees, depended on the homes of fellow Christians, as passages like 3 John 5-8 show. When Peter says 'without complaining', he knows how costly it was to open a small house to strangers.

The meeting of the church was itself the setting for the gifts of verse 11. Believers met in homes, and speaking and serving were things done in a few rooms among people who knew each other well.
context.canonical:
The call to stop living as the Gentiles did takes up a theme that runs through the New Testament. Paul tells the Ephesians not to walk as the Gentiles do, Ephesians 4:17-19, and reminds the Romans that the night is nearly over and that deeds of darkness belong to the past, Romans 13:11-14, where drunkenness and carousing appear in the very same vocabulary. Peter's list is a standard apostolic form of the 'once you were, but now' pattern, found also in 1 Corinthians 6:9-11 and Titus 3:3-7.

The Judge of the living and the dead is a phrase that comes from the early preaching of the apostles. Peter himself said in Acts 10:42 that Jesus was appointed by God to judge the living and the dead, and Paul charges Timothy in the same words in 2 Timothy 4:1. Judgment is entrusted to Christ, John 5:22-27, so the people who insult believers will answer to the very One they reject.

Love's covering of sins echoes Proverbs 10:12, where love covers all offenses, and James 5:20 uses a similar idea of turning a sinner back and covering a multitude of sins. Neither text teaches that our love earns forgiveness before God; the New Testament is clear that forgiveness rests on Christ's blood, 1:18-19. The text speaks of how love acts toward the failings of others, as Colossians 3:13 and Matthew 18:21-35 also teach.

The teaching on gifts parallels Romans 12:3-8, 1 Corinthians 12 to 14 and Ephesians 4:7-16, where each believer is given grace to serve the body. Peter's contribution is his steward language, which resembles Jesus' parables of the faithful and wise manager in Luke 12:42-48 and of the talents in Matthew 25:14-30, and Paul's own self-description in 1 Corinthians 4:1-2.

The doxology of verse 11 is part of a pattern in which praise to God is the climax of the New Testament's teaching, as at Romans 11:36 and Jude 1:24-25.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Peter writes to make the readers' ordinary days count. They felt the pressure of a hostile culture, and the temptation was to see their situation as a waiting room, in which nothing mattered until they were vindicated. He says the opposite: the period between now and the end is the time in which you are meant to live for God's will, to love, and to give. The nearness of the end does not suspend life; it clarifies it.

He also wants them to hear a rebuke of their enemies without any note of revenge. The mockers will give an account to Him who is ready to judge, and this is said so that believers may leave judgment where it belongs and carry on. Their calling is to live well, not to retaliate.

In the second part, he is building a community. Love, hospitality and gifts are the means by which an unwelcome minority becomes a family. A church that is despised outside must be generous inside, and Peter's commands are meant to produce a place where no one is left to bear pressure alone.

The two questions that run through the passage are what to do with the past and what to do with the future. For the past, the answer is that it is settled and should be left. For the future, the answer is to be sober, prayerful, loving and useful, and to do it all so that God, and not the believer, is praised. Peter wants his readers to understand that the glory of God is the end of everything ordinary, including a meal set before a stranger.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Verses 1 to 6 describe a change in life and give one command, to arm oneself. The description of the Gentile life in verse 3 is a report of what the readers once did, not a program for how to treat those who still do it. Peter does not tell believers to condemn, avoid or fight such people, but to live differently and to expect to be misunderstood.

The statement that the end is near is a description of the situation, and the commands that follow it are prescriptive. It would be a misuse to turn the nearness of the end into a basis for predicting dates. Peter uses it to call for steady, practical behavior, and the church has always done well to follow that example.

Verses 8 to 11 are plain commands that apply today without adjustment. Love deeply, welcome people without grumbling, use whatever you have received. The word 'whatever' matters: the instruction does not assume any particular gift and does not list them. Peter's two categories, speaking and serving, cover every kind of ministry from preaching to practical help.

The passage does not tell us how many gifts there are, how they are discovered or how they relate to office in the church, and it would be wrong to build such a system from it. What it does give is the attitude: gifts are received, held in trust and given away, and they always point to God.

debates.question: What does anyone who has suffered in the body is done with sin mean, verse 1?

views.label: A settled resolve to suffer rather than sin
views.case: To arm oneself with Christ's mind is to be so committed to God's will that one would rather suffer than sin. Whoever has made that break has decisively turned from the old life; suffering for righteousness marks the end of sin's reign.

views.label: Union with Christ's death to sin
views.case: Others hear an echo of dying with Christ: the believer who has suffered with Christ has, in principle, died to sin's dominion, as in Romans 6. Either way the point is a real break with sin, not sinless perfection.

debates.bearing: Both readings affirm a decisive turning from sin grounded in Christ, not a claim that believers never sin again. The armed, suffering resolve of the Christian is incompatible with a settled life of sin.

debates.question: Who are those now dead to whom the gospel was preached, verse 6?

views.label: Believers who heard the gospel and have since died
views.case: The most common reading: they heard the good news while alive, and though they have died, judged as all men are by bodily death, they live before God in the spirit. The verse comforts a church whose members were dying under pressure.

views.label: A proclamation connected to Christ's descent
views.case: Some link it to 3:19, seeing a proclamation to the departed. Yet even here orthodox readers deny a second chance after death; the emphasis remains that the gospel secures life with God beyond bodily death.

debates.bearing: Both guard against the idea of a second chance after death. The verse assures believers that death does not defeat those who received the gospel; judged in the body, they nonetheless live to God in the spirit.

debates.question: Whose sins does love cover, verse 8?

views.label: The sins of others, which love forgives and does not broadcast
views.case: The proverb behind the line speaks of love covering offenses instead of stirring up strife, Proverbs 10:12. Read this way, believers who love deeply overlook and forgive the faults of fellow believers, which makes unity possible in a community under pressure.

views.label: The lover's own sins, because love shows a forgiven heart
views.case: Some old interpreters heard in the line a promise that loving others brings God's forgiveness to the one who loves. Most careful readers reject this, since 1:18-19 grounds forgiveness in Christ's blood alone, but they allow that love is the evidence of a forgiven heart.

views.label: Love that restores the wanderer
views.case: James 5:20 speaks of turning a sinner from his error and so covering a multitude of sins. On this view the covering is the work of bringing a straying brother back, so that his sins are dealt with and not left to fester.

debates.bearing: The first reading best suits the immediate context of hospitality without grumbling. All three agree that love is costly, that it never excuses sin, and that God's own forgiveness rests on Christ and not on our efforts.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb in verse 1 for 'arm yourselves' comes from the word for weapons, hoplon, which Paul uses in Romans 6:13 and 13:12 and 2 Corinthians 10:4. Peter pictures the believer taking up the mind of Christ as a soldier takes up arms. The word 'resolve' in the same verse means a thought or intention, so the weapon is a way of thinking: the firm purpose to follow Christ even if it costs.

The catalog in verse 3 includes a word for unbridled indulgence, aselgeia, which Paul uses in Romans 13:13 alongside carousing, and a word for the revel, komos, which appears in Galatians 5:21 in the same company. The word 'flood' in verse 4 is a rare image of an outpouring or overflow, a picture of a stream pressing in one direction. And the Gentiles 'consider it strange', from the verb that elsewhere describes being surprised by a stranger or a guest, the same family as the 'strange' in 4:12.

The verb for 'heap abuse' in verse 4 is the one from which we get blasphemy, here used of speech against believers. In the next verse, 'the living and the dead' is a fixed expression found in Acts 10:42 and 2 Timothy 4:1, and 'give an account' is the language of accounting that Peter shares with Hebrews 13:17.

In verse 6 the verb 'preached' is euangelizo, to bring good news, and it is in the passive form and a past tense, 'was preached', which fits a gospel that was heard at a definite time. The BSB footnote notes that 'those who are now dead' can also be 'to those who are dead'.

In verse 7 two words describe the clear head. One is the verb used in 1:13 and 5:8 for being sober, and the other is a verb for sound judgment. Peter links them to prayer. The verb for 'love deeply' in verse 8 is built on a noun meaning stretched or intense, found in 1:22 and in Acts 12:5 of the church's earnest prayer. And 'covers', in 'love covers a multitude of sins', is the verb used in James 5:20.

The Greek behind 'manifold' in verse 10 is poikilos, 'many-colored' or 'varied', which is the same word Peter used in 1:6 for the various trials believers face. The grace of God is as many-sided as the troubles of life. The word 'steward', oikonomos, means a household manager who administers what belongs to someone else, as in Luke 12:42, Luke 16:1-8 and 1 Corinthians 4:1-2. The word for 'gift', charisma, is formed from charis, grace, so a gift is grace made concrete.

In verse 11, the phrase 'words of God' translates logia theou, which in Romans 3:2 refers to the sacred utterances entrusted to Israel. Speech in the church is to carry that weight. The word for the 'strength God provides' comes from a verb related to choregeo, to supply, as in 2 Corinthians 9:10, which originally described a person who funded a chorus. God is the sponsor; the believer is the performer.

typology.type: The steward over the Master's house
typology.fulfillment: From Genesis 2:15, where Adam is placed in the garden to work and keep it, to the servants in the parables of Jesus, God's people are managers of what belongs to another. Joseph over Potiphar's house, Genesis 39:4-6, is an Old Testament picture of faithful management. In the church, every believer is a steward of grace, and Christ is the Master who will return, Luke 12:42-44. The correspondence is that of trust and accountability. It falls short in that the steward owns nothing and earns nothing; he gives back what was first given.

Israel's warriors armed themselves for the battles of the LORD, and the prophets spoke of God as a warrior, Isaiah 59:17. Peter uses military language for a moral struggle, as Paul does in Ephesians 6:10-18. The pattern is fulfilled in Christ, who fought sin and death and won, and believers arm themselves with His mind. The type is limited, since the weapons here are not swords but patience and holiness, 2 Corinthians 10:3-4.

typology.type: The day of the LORD and the Judge of the living and the dead
typology.fulfillment: The prophets described a day when the LORD would judge the nations and rescue His people, Joel 2:31-32 and Malachi 4:1-3. Peter says the Judge is ready and that He is Jesus, Acts 10:42. The expectation that was national and distant becomes personal and near. What remains unresolved is the timing, which no passage settles and which Peter does not try to fix; he is content to say that the Judge is ready and that believers must live accordingly.

typology.type: Hospitality as a sign of the household of God
typology.fulfillment: Abraham welcomed three strangers at Mamre and entertained the LORD, Genesis 18:1-8, and Hebrews 13:2 says that some have entertained angels without knowing it. Hospitality in the early church was how the family of God was visible in practice. It is fulfilled in Christ's own welcome of sinners and in the marriage supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:9. The earthly table is a foretaste, not the feast itself.

study.christ:
The passage begins with Christ's suffering as the ground and pattern for believers. 'Since Christ suffered in His body' echoes 2:21 and 3:18, and sets the believer's own bodily suffering inside His. The decisive break with sin that Peter describes is not self-improvement but participation in the One who died to sin once for all. In Romans 6:10-11 Paul says that the death He died He died to sin, and that believers are to consider themselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus. Peter's armed resolve is the application of that fact.

The passage then leads to Christ as Judge. The 'Judge of the living and the dead' is Jesus Himself, according to Acts 10:42 and 2 Timothy 4:1, and John 5:22 says that the Father has entrusted all judgment to the Son. This is a comfort to the slandered. The One who stood before an unjust tribunal now sits as the Judge, and those who mock believers will stand before Him. It is also a solemn truth for believers, who also give account, 1 Peter 1:17.

It leads to Christ through the idea of grace. The 'manifold grace of God' is the grace that came with Him. Paul says that grace was given to each of us 'according to the measure of Christ's gift', Ephesians 4:7, and that the Son ascended and gave gifts to His people, Ephesians 4:8-11. Every gift of service is a gift of the risen Lord, and every act of service is done in His strength.

It leads to Christ as the mediator of glory. 'In all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ' says that all praise to God passes through the Son, who is the way to the Father, John 14:6. The final doxology, 'to whom be the glory and the power forever and ever', most naturally refers to Jesus Christ, the nearest name, and if so it is one of the New Testament's direct acts of worship addressed to Him, like 2 Peter 3:18 and Revelation 1:5-6.

He is also the model of love that covers. At the cross He bore the sins of many in His body, 2:24, and that is the deepest reason believers can cover one another's failings. Their love is not their own invention; it is a reflection of the love they have received.

A caution applies. Peter's steward language does not require that every steward in a parable be Christ, nor every household manager a picture of Him. What the passage gives is Christ as the pattern of suffering, the power of service, the Judge and the One through whom God is glorified.
study.god:
The passage shows us a God who judges with readiness. He is 'ready to judge the living and the dead', a phrase that suggests not delay but preparedness. For readers under insult, it means they do not need to defend themselves to the last word. For those who live heedlessly, it is a sober truth. Judgment is not an arbitrary outburst; it is the settled response of the Creator to a world that belongs to Him, and the mockers' account is to be given to Him, not to the church.

He is the God whose will is a standard for ordinary life. Peter contrasts 'human passions' with 'the will of God', and the second is not a mysterious private plan but the pattern of holy, loving, useful living laid out in the rest of the passage. His will is knowable and livable, and it is the good the believer was made for.

He is the giver. The word 'manifold' says that His grace is many-sided, with enough variety to meet any trouble and to equip any servant. The gifts are described as received, and the strength for service is 'provided' by God. Nothing the believer has is self-generated. This is a doctrine of divine generosity that leaves no room for pride or for despair at having too little.

He is the God who is glorified. The purpose of everything is His glory through Jesus Christ, and the doxology ascribes to Him both glory and power forever. The passage's own movement shows what that means: the glory of God is not served by solitary heroics but by a community that prays, loves, welcomes and serves.

He is the Lord of time. The end of all things is near because He has set a goal for history, and He is bringing it on. The believer is placed within a story with a destination, which is why sobriety and prayer make sense.

He holds judgment and mercy together. The same chapter speaks of those who will answer to Him and of the gospel preached even to the dead, so that those who died in Christ live to Him in the spirit. The Judge is also the One who gave His Son. The right response is worship: to hold ourselves accountable, to receive His grace, and to hand it on.

crossReferences.note: Believers died with Christ to sin and are alive to God in Him. This is the doctrinal root of Peter's being done with sin: the break is not a heroic effort but the working out of a death and resurrection already shared with Christ.

Paul says the night is nearly over and the day is at hand, and tells believers to put aside orgies, drunkenness and sensuality and to put on the Lord Jesus. It uses the same pairing of nearness and conduct as Peter and the same list of vices.

Peter told Cornelius that Jesus was appointed by God as judge of the living and the dead. The phrase in 1 Peter 4:5 comes from the apostles' regular preaching, and identifies the coming Judge with the crucified and risen Lord.

Hatred stirs up strife but love covers all offenses. This is the source of the proverb Peter uses, and it shows that the covering is about how love deals with the faults of others, forgiving and not publicizing them.

Whoever turns a sinner from his error will save him from death and cover a multitude of sins. It uses the same verb and phrase as Peter, and shows that the covering is a way of restoration among believers.

Jesus asks who is the faithful and wise manager whom the master will put in charge of his household. The reward is more responsibility. It gives the shape of Peter's steward: trusted, accountable and expected to give each person what is due in its time.

There are different gifts but the same Spirit, given to each for the common good. Paul's emphasis on diversity and shared purpose matches Peter's manifold grace and the call to use whatever one has received for others.

Gifts differ according to the grace given, and the list includes serving and teaching, followed at once by love without hypocrisy and sharing with the saints in need. The sequence of gifts, love and hospitality matches Peter's own order.

Keep loving one another as brothers, and do not neglect to show hospitality, for some have entertained angels unawares. It shows how hospitality was bound up with brotherly love in the first generation of the church.

Peter had already described believers as grieved by various trials, using the same word that now describes God's grace as manifold. The echo suggests that for every kind of trial there is a matching form of grace.

study.oneStory:
The passage touches a question that the Bible raises at the very beginning: what is humanity for? In Genesis 1:28 and 2:15 men and women are made to rule and keep God's world under His authority, to be stewards in the garden. The fall turned stewards into rivals, and the story that follows is the story of people serving their own passions and their own gods. Peter's catalog of the old life in verse 3 is the long result.

Redemption in Christ restores the vocation. Believers are brought out of that life and set back into stewardship, not of a garden now but of grace. Their calling is to receive, to hold in trust and to give away, all for the glory of God. That is the original purpose of humanity recovered in a redeemed people.

The Old Testament spoke of a day of the LORD when God would act decisively. Peter says the end of all things is near, and the Judge is ready. Between Christ's first coming and His return the church lives in the time that remains, and that time is not wasted but given for love, prayer, welcome and service. The delay is a space for mercy, as 2 Peter 3:9 says.

The passage also lines up with the gospel's reach. 'The gospel was preached even to those now dead' says that the message of Christ stretches across time, so that those who heard it and have died are not lost to God. Death, the last enemy, has not undone those who belong to Him.

The new creation completes what the passage begins. Believers who served as stewards will hear 'well done, good and faithful servant' and enter the joy of their Master, Matthew 25:21, and every act of love covered in secret will be seen in the light. The hospitality offered in cramped rooms is a small picture of the great table at which God will host His people, Revelation 19:9, and the praise which Peter ends with, glory and power forever, will become the unbroken song of a creation in which God is all in all, Revelation 5:13.

quiz.q: What does it mean to arm yourselves with the same resolve as Christ?

options.text: To be so committed to God's will that you would rather suffer than sin.
options.note: Verse 1: the armed resolve is a decisive break with the old life of sin.

options.text: To seek out suffering for its own sake.
options.note: The point is willingness to suffer rather than sin, not seeking suffering itself.

options.text: To defend yourself aggressively against all opponents.
options.note: The weapon is a mind set on God's will, not aggression toward others.

options.text: To share Christ's death to sin and live for God.
options.note: True to the sense, though the answer should name the resolve to suffer rather than sin.

quiz.q: How do the readers' former companions react to their new life?

options.text: They think it strange and heap abuse on them for not joining the old excess.
options.note: Verse 4: withdrawal from debauchery draws ridicule and slander.

options.text: They admire and quickly imitate the change.
options.note: Peter says the opposite: they are surprised and abusive.

options.text: They ignore the believers entirely.
options.note: They do not ignore them; they revile them.

options.text: They are surprised and respond with insults.
options.note: True, though the answer should include that they will answer to the Judge.

quiz.q: What effect does the nearness of the end have, according to Peter?

options.text: It calls for clear-minded, sober prayer and fervent love, not panic.
options.note: Verses 7 to 8: the end fuels prayer and love, not speculation or fear.

options.text: It means believers should stop working and simply wait.
options.note: Peter calls for active love, hospitality, and service, not passivity.

options.text: It should provoke fearful calculation of dates.
options.note: The response is prayer and love, not date-setting.

options.text: It gives urgency to loving and serving one another.
options.note: True and close, though the answer should include clear-minded prayer as well.

quiz.q: How are believers to use the gifts they have received?

options.text: As stewards of God's manifold grace, using each gift to serve one another.
options.note: Verse 10: gifts are held in trust and deployed for others' good.

options.text: For personal display and recognition.
options.note: The gifts serve others and God's glory, not self-display.

options.text: Only if they feel especially talented.
options.note: Each one has received a gift to use; it is not for a gifted few only.

options.text: To build up the church according to what God has given.
options.note: True, though the answer should name stewardship of God's manifold grace.

quiz.q: What is the stated goal of all Christian speaking and serving?

options.text: That in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ.
options.note: Verse 11: God's glory through Christ is the aim, sealed with a doxology.

options.text: That the church may grow impressively large.
options.note: The goal is God's glory, not size or reputation.

options.text: That believers may be praised for their service.
options.note: The glory goes to God through Christ, not to the servant.

options.text: That the community may function smoothly.
options.note: Good order helps, but the stated goal is God's glory through Jesus Christ.

questions: Peter says you have spent enough time in the old way of living. What part of your former life is God calling you to leave firmly behind?
When others find your faith strange and mock your choices, how do you usually respond, and how might remembering the coming Judge steady you?
The end of all things is near. If you truly believed today might be near the end, what would you pray for, and whom would you love better?
Love covers a multitude of sins. Whose faults is God asking you to bear with in love rather than expose or resent?
You are a steward of some gift of God's grace. What has He given you, and how could you use it this week to serve someone else and glorify Him?

translationNotes.note: Done with sin renders a phrase meaning has ceased from sin; in context it describes the decisive break with the old life that marks one armed with Christ's resolve, not sinless perfection.
Those who are now dead most likely means believers who heard the gospel and have since died; judged as all are by bodily death, they nonetheless live to God in the spirit.
Manifold grace translates poikile charis, varied or many-colored grace, distributed as diverse gifts so that the whole church displays the fullness of God's giving.
